extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Platonic philosophy; literary critics and thinkers concerned with poetry, imitation, and moral education
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and normative claims for judging imitative poetry and its moral/epistemic effects, as argued in Plato's Republic (Books IX–X). Useful for assessing whether poetic/imitative art is truthful, educative, and conducive to a well-ordered soul or state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of imitative poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: All poetical imitations are ruinous to the understanding of the hearers, and the knowledge of their true nature is the only antidote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato asserts plainly that 'the rejection of imitative poetry... ought not to be received' because such imitations mislead the soul. He treats Homer and tragedians as prime examples and argues that understanding the true nature of imitation is necessary to counteract their harmful influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitators are thrice removed from the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitator (painter/poet) produces an image which is thrice removed from the form or truth: God (form) → maker (craftsman) → painter/poet (imitator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the bed analogy (ideal bed vs. carpenter's bed vs. painter's picture), the text emphasizes that poets produce appearances, not realities; therefore their works lack the truth and authority of the maker or the form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge hierarchy: user, maker, imitator
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three arts: the user (who has practical knowledge), the maker (who makes things and attains correct belief about them), and the imitator (who copies appearances and lacks genuine knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the flute-player (user) knows which flute is good and instructs the flute-maker; the painter cannot know the use and thus cannot truly judge excellence. This is used as a standard: authentic understanding of a subject (knowledge) is required for authoritative art about it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets should possess subject-matter knowledge (otherwise mere appearance)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one truly knows what one depicts (e.g., war, politics, education), one would aim at realities rather than only image-making; lack of such knowledge makes a poet an imitator of appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates questions Homer: did he ever legislate, teach, or improve any city? If poets had real knowledge they would have had followers or practical achievements. The absence of such evidence is a test for whether a poetic work is grounded in knowledge or mere imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation appeals to and strengthens the inferior parts of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitative art addresses and nourishes the irrational/passional parts of the soul (the many-headed monster, the lion, the serpent), rather than the rational/calculating principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because poets tend to imitate passions and fitful temperaments, they cultivate those inferior elements, creating imbalance; good art should instead foster the calculating, rational principle and harmonize the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's moral impact: it can harm by encouraging inappropriate sympathies
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry that excites pity, lamentation, or other passions encourages spectators to take pleasure in behavior they would condemn in themselves, thereby transmitting some evil to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: audiences delight in another's drawn-out lamentation in poetry, yet in real life they prize patience and would abominate such conduct. This mismatch shows how poetry can inculcate undesirable responses and weaken moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should serve the harmony and governance of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper aim of education/art is to cultivate the higher element (reason/divine in man) and set up a guardian-ruler in the heart, so that the beastly parts are kept in order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates argues that laws and education have the purpose of establishing the higher principle in children; similarly, art should foster temperance, wisdom and harmony rather than relax or inflame lower impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude imitative poets from a well-ordered State
rubrics_metrics.description: Because imitative poets 'awaken and nourish and strengthen the feelings and impair the reason,' they should be refused admission into a well-ordered city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a concrete policy conclusion: poets are likened to painters (inferior offspring) and are judged unfit for the ideal state's education because their work implants an 'evil constitution' in souls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate art by its relation to use/purpose (functionality principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence, beauty, or truth of every thing (structure, animate or inanimate, or human action) is relative to the use for which nature or the artist has intended it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus the correct assessor is the user/practitioner (e.g., horseman for bits/reins, flute-player for flutes). When judging artistic depiction of a practice, preference should be given to works informed by practical knowledge of that use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish appearance from reality; value reality over ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: The painter and poet imitate appearance, not reality; if an artist could create the original or reality, he would not devote himself to mere appearance-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art that prioritizes ornament, melody, or rhythm over truthful representation of realities risks deceiving the ignorant and failing to contribute to human improvement; the true aim should be the reality the imitation stands for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure goodness by proximity to law and reason (pleasure as diagnostic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures and desires are measured by their distance from philosophy, law and reason: royal/orderly desires are nearest to true pleasure, tyrannical/lustful desires farthest; justice yields truer and far superior pleasure than injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socratic/arithmetic metaphors (e.g., the tyrant living '729 times' more painfully than the king) provide a way to evaluate lives, pleasures, and political constitutions by their conformity to reason and law rather than by apparent gains of power or wealth.
